verdict.rationale: Two pieces of the proposition have genuine lexical footing and two do not. Rule by a plurality of elders is attested: the word for elder (presbyteros) is plural and is appointed congregation by congregation (Acts 14:23, where the phrase is 'in each church' (kat ekklesian), Titus 1:5, Acts 20:17), and 1 Timothy 5:17 speaks of elders who rule well ('beautifully leading' (kalos proestotes)) with a subset laboring in word and teaching. Trans-local action (action reaching beyond a single congregation) is attested in Acts 15, where Antioch sends to the apostles and elders at Jerusalem, the body gathers ('come together' (synago)), and 'it seems good' ('it seems' (dokeo)) to issue a letter to Gentile churches. But the two pillars of the graded-court reading (the idea that elders sit in layered ranked councils) are lexically thin. The ruling verb 'to lead' or 'to manage' (proistemi) (8 occurrences) is polysemous (carrying more than one sense), ranging from governing (1 Thessalonians 5:12) through managing a household (1 Timothy 3:4-5, 12) to merely devoting oneself to good works (Titus 3:8, 14), so it does not by itself erect a ruling office. The collective noun 'body of elders' (presbyterion) occurs 3 times, and 2 of those (Luke 22:66, Acts 22:5) denote the Jewish Sanhedrin (the Jewish ruling council), leaving only 1 Timothy 4:14 for a Christian body of elders acting together. Standing graded courts, a session-presbytery-assembly chain (the layered local-regional-national council ladder), and a teaching-versus-ruling two-office split are never named, and the evaluative tail about over-institutionalisation (the worry that the system becomes too rigid an institution) is not a lexical datum (not a fact the words alone can supply). The affirmable core and the unattested superstructure (the unsupported upper layers of the system) pull apart, so the verdict is disputed.

scripture.force: Paul and Barnabas appointed elders for them in each church ('elders in each church' (πρεσβυτέρους κατ ἐκκλησίαν)). The plural object 'elders' and the distributive 'in each' phrase (κατ ἐκκλησίαν, meaning church by church) locate a plurality of elders within each local assembly or church (ekklesia, meaning either an assembly or a church). This grounds elder-rule by a plurality but ties the office to the single assembly, not to a higher grade above it.

Titus is left to appoint elders city by city ('elders city by city' (πρεσβυτέρους κατὰ πόλιν)), reproducing the Acts 14:23 distributive pattern (the per-locale appointment pattern) with the plural noun 'elders'. The appointing is delegated and per-locale, which supports plural local eldership and is neutral toward, but does not erect, a standing court over multiple cities.

Let the elders who rule well ('the beautifully leading elders' (οἱ καλῶς προεστῶτες πρεσβύτεροι)) be counted worthy of double honour, especially those who labour in word and teaching. The verb 'to lead' or 'to manage' (προΐστημι, proistemi) attributes governing to elders, the strongest single text for elder-rule. The 'especially' clause (μάλιστα, malista, meaning 'most of all') marks a subset who labour in teaching, which can be read as degrees of labour within one plural body rather than two constitutional offices, so the verse supports elder-rule but does not by itself split a teaching elder from a ruling elder.

An overseer must be one who manages his own household well ('beautifully managing his own household' (τοῦ ἰδίου οἴκου καλῶς προϊστάμενον)). The same verb 'to lead' or 'to manage' (προΐστημι, proistemi) here governs a household, not a church court. This is the polysemy datum (the fact that the word carries more than one sense): the ruling verb carries a household-management sense alongside any governing sense, so 'to lead or manage' (προΐστημι, proistemi) alone cannot establish a graded ecclesiastical office (a ranked church office).

Those who have believed should be careful to devote themselves to good works ('to devote oneself to good works' (προΐστασθαι καλῶν ἔργων)). Here 'to lead or manage' (προΐστημι, proistemi) means to attend to or maintain, with no governing sense at all. Across its 8 occurrences the verb spans governing, managing a household, and devoting oneself to a task, so its appearance in 1 Timothy 5:17 does not lexically guarantee a ruling-office reading.

Do not neglect the gift given you through prophecy with the laying on of hands of the body of elders ('with the laying on of the hands of the body of elders' (μετὰ ἐπιθέσεως τῶν χειρῶν τοῦ πρεσβυτερίου)). This is the one occurrence where 'body of elders' (πρεσβυτέριον, presbyterion) denotes a Christian eldership acting as a single corporate body, the lexical kernel (the word-level seed of evidence) for elders functioning together rather than singly. It describes a collective ordination act (a joint commissioning), not a standing graded court ranked above local assemblies.

The body of elders of the people ('the body of elders of the people' (τὸ πρεσβυτέριον τοῦ λαοῦ)) gathered and led Jesus into their council ('council' (συνέδριον, synedrion)). Here 'body of elders' (πρεσβυτέριον, presbyterion) names the Jewish Sanhedrin (the Jewish ruling council). Two of the three canon uses of the term (this and Acts 22:5) refer to that Jewish body, so the noun is not primarily a Christian church-order term, which thins its weight as a basis for a Christian graded court.

After no small dissension at Antioch the assembly (ekklesia, meaning either an assembly or a church) appoints Paul, Barnabas, and certain others to go up to the apostles and elders ('to the apostles and elders' (πρὸς τοὺς ἀποστόλους καὶ πρεσβυτέρους)) at Jerusalem about this question. The verse establishes a deliberative referral (a formal sending of a question for joint discussion) from one local body to a recognised body in another city, the lexical kernel (the word-level seed) of any trans-local consultation reading (any reading that says churches conferred across cities).

The apostles and the elders were gathered together ('were gathered together' (συνήχθησαν, a form of synago, meaning to come together)) to see about this matter. The verb 'to come together' (συνάγω, synago) is the ordinary verb for assembling and is used elsewhere of crowds and synagogues; it describes a convened body for one question, not a permanent court with defined appellate grades (defined layers of higher-court appeal). The convened body is apostles plus elders deliberating jointly.

Then it seemed good ('it seemed' (ἔδοξε, a form of dokeo)) to the apostles and the elders with the whole assembly or church ('with the whole church' (σὺν ὅλῃ τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ)) to send chosen men. The decision verb 'it seems' (δοκέω, dokeo) is the ordinary verb for what seems good or right, used 63 times across the canon for human opinion, not a technical juridical term (not a specialised legal term). The 'with' phrase (σύν) joins the whole congregation to the apostles and elders, which both supports a corporate conciliar reading (a reading where the whole body deliberates as a council) and complicates a top-down graded-court reading in which only ordained officers decide.

It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us ('it seemed to the Holy Spirit and to us' (ἔδοξεν τῷ πνεύματι τῷ ἁγίῳ καὶ ἡμῖν)) to lay no greater burden. The council frames its conclusion as a Spirit-led judgment issued with trans-local force (binding effect reaching beyond one congregation) to Gentile congregations, yet it grounds the authority in the apostolic 'we', which is non-transferable (cannot be passed on to later officers), rather than in a perpetual institutional grade (a permanent ranked office).

From Miletus Paul sent to Ephesus and called the elders of the assembly or church ('the elders of the church' (τοὺς πρεσβυτέρους τῆς ἐκκλησίας)). A plurality of elders is tied to a single named church, again locating the office at the congregational level rather than constituting a court above it.

Peter exhorts the elders as a fellow-elder ('fellow-elder' (συμπρεσβύτερος, sympresbyteros)), a hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible). The collegial 'with' prefix (συν, syn, meaning together) places the apostle alongside the elders rather than above them in a graded chain, which complicates a reading that grounds higher ruling grades in apostolic precedent.

Shepherd the flock of God among you ('the flock among you' (τὸ ἐν ὑμῖν ποίμνιον)), exercising oversight ('overseeing' (ἐπισκοποῦντες, a form of episkopos, meaning overseer or bishop)). The flock is the local one 'among you', and the participle (the -ing verb form) equates elder-work with overseeing. The terms 'elder' (πρεσβύτερος, presbyteros) and the overseeing verb describe one function, not two graded offices, which complicates a teaching-elder versus ruling-elder taxonomy (the proposed two-office classification).

complicating_texts.resolution: The ruling verb 'to lead or manage' (προΐστημι, proistemi) governs a household here and means to devote oneself in Titus 3:8, so across its 8 canon occurrences it is polysemous (carrying more than one sense) between governing, managing a home, and attending to a task. Because the one elder-rule text (1 Timothy 5:17) uses this same verb, the verb cannot by itself establish a distinct ruling office or a graded court (a ranked appellate council). This polysemy is weighed as a reason the graded-court superstructure (the upper layers of ranked councils) is lexically underdetermined (not fixed by the words themselves), so the verdict stays disputed.

'Body of elders' (πρεσβυτέριον, presbyterion) denotes the Jewish Sanhedrin (the Jewish ruling council) here and in Acts 22:5, leaving only 1 Timothy 4:14 for a Christian body of elders. The collective-body sense applied to the church therefore rests on a single occurrence describing a joint laying on of hands, not on a recurring term for a standing graded assembly (a permanent ranked council). The verdict treats this thin attestation as a reason a presbytery-as-court reading (reading the body of elders as a formal court) is not lexically forced.

The inclusion of the whole assembly or church ('with the whole church' (σὺν ὅλῃ τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ)) and the ordinary decision verb 'it seems' (δοκέω, dokeo) show the Jerusalem deliberation was corporate and not framed in technical juridical language (specialised legal vocabulary). This complicates a strict graded-court reading in which only ordained elders decide, and it equally undercuts the over-institutionalisation charge (the worry that the system grows into too rigid an institution), so it pulls the verdict toward disputed rather than a clean affirm or deny.

'Fellow-elder' (συμπρεσβύτερος, sympresbyteros) presents apostolic authority as collegial with the eldership (alongside the elders as peers) rather than as the apex of a graded chain. Since the proposition leans on Acts 15 apostolic precedent for higher courts, this collegial self-description weakens the inference from apostolic precedent to a perpetual ruling grade (a permanent higher rank). It is addressed by noting the apostolic role in Acts 15 was unique and non-transferable (cannot be passed on), leaving the trans-local question (the question of authority reaching across congregations) genuinely open.

variants.note: Acts, 1 Timothy, Titus, Luke, and 1 Peter all lie outside the published CBGM (the modern text-critical method) 3 John sample, so ECM status (the status against the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) is treated as shadow and no loaded apparatus (no full set of variant readings) was examined. Standard apparatus marks minor readings in Acts 15 (for example word order in 15:7 and the article ('the') before 'elders' (πρεσβύτεροι, presbyteroi) at 15:23) and the omission of 'overseeing' (ἐπισκοποῦντες, a form of episkopos) at 1 Peter 5:2, but none touches the presence of apostles and elders, the verbs 'it seems' (δοκέω, dokeo) and 'to come together' (συνάγω, synago), the noun 'body of elders' (πρεσβυτέριον, presbyterion), or the verb 'to lead or manage' (προΐστημι, proistemi) on which the verdict turns, so the verdict holds across plausible readings.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads 1 Timothy 5:17 (elders who rule, 'to lead or manage' (προΐστημι, proistemi)) plus the plural 'elder' (presbyteros) appointed per congregation, the collective 'body of elders' (πρεσβυτέριον, presbyterion) acting together in 1 Timothy 4:14, and Acts 15 as a trans-local assembly of elders (a body of elders reaching across congregations) binding member churches, taking these as the pattern for graded courts (ranked councils) of teaching and ruling elders. At its strongest this lens has real lexical purchase: elder-rule, a corporate body of elders, and trans-local conciliar action (joint council action reaching beyond one congregation) are each attested. Its lexical limit is that 'to lead or manage' (προΐστημι, proistemi) is polysemous (carries more than one sense), 'body of elders' (πρεσβυτέριον, presbyterion) as a Christian body occurs once, and standing appellate grades (permanent higher-court ranks) and the two-office split are never named.

Reads 'in each church' (κατ ἐκκλησίαν, kat ekklesian) eldership (Acts 14:23, Titus 1:5, Acts 20:17), the 'flock among you' (1 Peter 5:2), and the whole assembly or church included in the decision (Acts 15:22, 'with the whole church' (σὺν ὅλῃ τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ)) as locating authority in each local assembly, treating Acts 15 as a one-time apostolic consultation rather than a perpetual court. At its strongest this lens shows the eldership consistently anchored to the single congregation and the congregation present in the great decision. Its lexical limit is that the same data does not forbid trans-local consultation (a consultation reaching across congregations), which Acts 15 plainly records.

The single-function fusion of 'elder' (πρεσβύτερος, presbyteros) and the overseeing verb in 1 Peter 5:1-2, and the collegial 'fellow-elder' (συμπρεσβύτερος, sympresbyteros), tell against a separate monarchical bishop grade (a separate single-bishop rank) as much as against a separate ruling-elder grade, so the cited corpus is neutral toward this lens. Its strongest lexical foothold is the delegate roles of Titus and Timothy appointing elders across cities, which the vocabulary leaves open between a permanent office and a temporary apostolic errand.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict turns on whether Acts 15 plus 1 Timothy 5:17 and 4:14 are read as institutional precedent for standing graded courts (permanent ranked councils) or as elder-rule and corporate elder-action that the words do not rank into a session-presbytery-assembly chain (a local-regional-national council ladder). Two attested patterns, local plural eldership and a single trans-local consultation (a one-off consultation reaching beyond one congregation), are present in the corpus, and the vocabulary does not subordinate one to the other, which is why competing lenses each gain partial purchase.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Rule by a plurality of elders and a single trans-local consultation (a one-off consultation reaching beyond one congregation) among elders both have lexical footing in the New Testament, and the question is whether graded standing courts (permanent ranked councils) of distinct teaching and ruling elders, in a session, presbytery, and general assembly chain (a local-regional-national council ladder), and their effect on local-assembly authority, can be established from the text.
stem_audit.notes: The original stem embeds an evaluative conclusion (tends toward over-institutionalisation (becoming too rigid an institution) and erodes local-assembly autonomy (the self-governance of the local congregation)) and a specific institutional taxonomy (session, presbytery, general assembly, ruling versus teaching elders, that is, the layered council ladder and the two-office split) that the lexicon (the word-evidence base) cannot confirm or measure. The verdict was derived on the original stem, but the neutralized form isolates the parts the lexical store can actually address, namely the presence or absence of elder-rule, a corporate body of elders, trans-local consultation, and graded offices in the cited texts. Judged on the same lexical footing as the sibling congregational and episcopal polity questions, all three land disputed because the same small vocabulary band underdetermines the system each erects (does not fix the system the proposition builds).

lay_summary: The lexical evidence (the evidence from the actual words) gives a split picture, which is why this proposition lands as disputed. Part of it has real support in the words. The term for elder, 'elder' (presbyteros), is always plural and is appointed congregation by congregation in Acts 14:23 and Titus 1:5, and 1 Timothy 5:17 speaks of elders who rule well, using a verb (proistemi, meaning to lead or manage) that does mean to lead. Acts 15 plainly records a trans-local event (an event reaching beyond one congregation): the church at Antioch sends men up to the apostles and elders at Jerusalem, that body gathers, and a letter goes out to Gentile congregations framed as seeming good to the Holy Spirit and to us. So elder-rule and a council that reaches beyond one congregation are both attested. The trouble is that the two pillars of the graded-court picture (the picture of layered ranked councils) are lexically thin. The verb translated rule in 1 Timothy 5:17, proistemi, occurs only eight times, and across those eight it slides between governing a church, managing one's own household, and simply devoting oneself to good works, so the word alone cannot build a ruling office. The noun for a body of elders, presbyterion, occurs only three times, and two of those name the Jewish Sanhedrin (the Jewish ruling council) that condemned Jesus, leaving just one verse where it means a Christian eldership acting together, and there it describes a joint laying on of hands, not a standing court. The decision verb in Acts 15 is the ordinary word for what seems good (dokeo), not a legal term, and the whole assembly or church (ekklesia) shares in the sending, which works against a closed court of officers. Nowhere do the words name a layered session, presbytery, and general assembly, nor do they separate a teaching elder from a ruling elder. The claim that such a system tends toward over-institutionalisation (becoming too rigid an institution) is a value judgment the words cannot weigh. Because the affirmable core and the unnamed superstructure (the unsupported upper layers) pull apart, the honest lexical reading is that the proposition is materially contested.
